items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: I joined Count Basie in 1938... When I first joined the band I was 19 and he just took a liking to me... everybody in the Count Basie band had played with Bennie Moten’s band.

ctx.x: Is it a skill that you learned — how did you learn that skill? Can you describe that?

Yes, because in my era, as you know, there was a lot of prejudice toward the musicians because we couldn’t play in a studio band, they had radio bands that were getting paid weekly, they were on a salary. They had musicians here at Fox Studio, MGM, Metro Goldwyn Mayer, they were all on staff. And they got paid whenever they worked or played. But they didn’t have black musicians at the time. So our only course was to play solos. And when you picked up your horn, you’d get you a “Georgia Brown” or something,…

to do. They could be with their families, you know? But we had to take to the road. And as I was telling Wynton Marsalis, I made a CD with him last week. And I told him that you know there were quite a few good, legitimate trumpet players years ago, but they had no place to play. There was one guy, Russell Smith, he was the greatest student Bach had. He learned the trumpet, oh there was no kind of concert trumpet he couldn’t play. But he couldn’t get a job. So he had to go with Fletcher Henderson for the rest of…

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Of course when I joined Count Basie’s band in 1938… that was my beginning of a career with Count Basie.

ctx.x: Can you give us some insights as to how he worked in the studio, was he a fast worker, did he do a lot of takes?

No, he didn’t do too many takes. He knew what he wanted to do before he got there. Evidently, he had gotten with Sy Oliver before the record date and Sy wrote the arrangements according to what Pops’ ideas were. So, we just ran through them, he didn’t take no time. It didn’t take any time at all for him to do that. I wouldn’t have cared anyway if he had taken 10 hours because I was having a ball up there, watching how he played. He used to come to hear me play when he’d come to California here, I had a little gig…

Ayres was the musical director. He used to come over and sit down and tell me a lot of jokes, ‘cause he and Basie were very good friends. He and Basie were very, very, very good friends. I didn’t know that so many of the older musicians were as tight as they were because the road was the only life that we knew. And I remember when Duke was very sick, they were making this “I Love You Madly” TV show here at Century City and I went out there and I was sitting with Basie and I found out that he and Duke had been…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: When I first went with Basie in 1938... Basie was only making $15.00 and he was the bandleader.

ctx.x: Yeah, remember the tune I wrote for Basie called 'Beaver Junction.' That was -- I staved there from the time I was 5 until I was 12.
Did you know your father at all? Do you remember him?

items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Well that was after I left the band. ... He was the “Holy Man.” ... they called him “The Chief.”

ctx.x: Where did he get the name “The Chief?” Do you remember that?
Well that was after I left the band.
